'''Zafra M. Lerman''' is an American chemist, educator, and humanitarian. She is the President of the Malta Conferences Foundation, which aims to promote peace by bringing together scientists from otherwise hostile countries to discuss science and foster international scientific and technical collaboration.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.maltaconferencesfoundation.org/index.html|title=Malta Conferences Foundation website|website=maltaconferencesfoundation.org|access-date=2015-06-18|archive-date=2016-04-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160405204458/http://maltaconferencesfoundation.org/index.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> From 1986 to 2010, she chaired the [[American Chemical Society]]'s Subcommittee on Scientific Freedom and Human Rights.<ref>In 2010, this Subcommittee was dissolved and its activities were absorbed into the other Subcommittees of the ACS' Committee on International Activities</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Linda|title=Human Rights And Science|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=August 24, 2009|volume=84|issue=34|pages=28–29|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/87/i34/Human-Rights-Science.html|access-date=16 January 2016}}</ref> She has been successful in preventing executions, releasing prisoners of conscience from jail and bringing dissidents to freedom.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lerman|first1=Zafra|title=Human Rights, Education, and Peace: A Personal Odyssey|journal=Journal of Chemical Education|date=September 6, 2012|volume=90|issue=1|pages=5–9|doi=10.1021/ed101063s}}</ref> She is the recipient of many awards for education and [[science diplomacy]], including the 1999 Presidential Award from U.S. President [[Bill Clinton|Clinton]],<ref name="ClintonAward" /> the 2005 [[Nyholm Prize for Education]] from the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (England),<ref name="Nyholm">{{cite web|title=Nyholm Prize for Education Previous Winners|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/NyholmPrizeEducation/PreviousWinners.asp|website=Royal Society of Chemistry (UK)|access-date=7 March 2016}}</ref> the 2015 [[AAAS Award for Science Diplomacy|Science Diplomacy Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)]],<ref name="AAAS Award">{{cite web|last1=Pinholster|first1=Ginger|title=Zafra M. Lerman Receives 2014 AAAS Award for Science Diplomacy - The award honors Lerman for promoting multinational scientific cooperation in the Middle East.|url=http://www.aaas.org/news/zafra-m-lerman-receives-2014-aaas-award-science-diplomacy|access-date=17 January 2016|website=American Association for the Advancement of Science}}</ref> the 2016 [[Andrei Sakharov Prize (APS)|Andrei Sakharov Award]] for human rights from the [[American Physical Society]] (APS),<ref name="SaharovPrize" /> the 2016 [[United Nations]] NOVUS Award for the [[Sustainable Development Goal 16|16th Sustainable Development Goal]]: Peace and Justice,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Zafra M. Lerman (Scientist) - NOVUS Award Ceremony, NOVUS Summit 2016|url=http://webtv.un.org/watch/zafra-m.-lerman-scientist-novus-award-ceremony-novus-summit-2016/5042173949001/?term=|access-date=2020-11-14|website=United Nations Web TV|language=en}}</ref>  the 2017 [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry]] Distinguished Women in Chemistry or Chemical Engineering Award,<ref>{{Cite web |title=IUPAC Distinguished Women in Chemistry or Chemical Engineering |url=https://iupac.org/what-we-do/awards/iupac-distinguished-women/ |access-date=2023-02-16 |website=IUPAC {{!}} International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry |language=en-US}}</ref> and the 2025 Cardozo School of Law’s 24th International Advocate for Peace Award.<ref name="cardozo.yu.edu">{{Cite web |title=Scientist Zafra Lerman To Receive Cardozo's 24th Annual International Advocate for Peace Award in March {{!}} Cardozo Law |url=https://cardozo.yu.edu/news/scientist-zafra-lerman-receive-cardozos-24th-annual-international-advocate-peace-award-march |access-date=2025-08-19 |website=cardozo.yu.edu |language=en}}</ref>

==Early career==
Lerman received a Ph.D. in chemistry from the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]] in [[Rehovot]], [[Israel]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Graduates: 50 Years of Excellence at the Feinberg Graduate School|date=2008|publisher=Weizmann Institute of Science Alumni Organization|location=Rehovot, Israel|url=http://www.weizmann.ac.il/alumni/pdf/The_Graduates.pdf|access-date=4 February 2016|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304111315/http://www.weizmann.ac.il/alumni/pdf/The_Graduates.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="LermanThesis">{{cite book|last1=Lerman|first1=Zafra|title=Ph.D. Thesis: Isotope Research|date=1969|publisher=Weizmann Institute of Science|location=Rehovot, Israel|url=http://lib-phds1.weizmann.ac.il/Dissertations/MARGOLIN_JACOBI_ZAFRA.pdf|access-date=4 February 2016|archive-date=30 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151130144727/http://lib-phds1.weizmann.ac.il/Dissertations/MARGOLIN_JACOBI_ZAFRA.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> She conducted research on isotope effects at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]],<ref name="LermanThesis" /><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Margolin|first1=Zafra|last2=Samuel|first2=D.|title=Carbon and oxygen isotope effects in the decarbonylation of benzoylformic acid in concentrated sulphuric acid|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society D: Chemical Communications|date=1970|volume=1970|issue=13|pages=802–803|doi=10.1039/C29700000802}}</ref> [[Cornell University]] and [[Northwestern University]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Olmstead|first1=William N.|last2=Margolin|first2=Zafra|last3=Bordwell|first3=Frederick G.|title=Acidities of water and simple alcohols in dimethyl sulfoxide solution|journal=Journal of Organic Chemistry|date=August 1980|volume=45|issue=16|pages=3295–3299|doi=10.1021/jo01304a032}}</ref> in the US, and the [[ETH Zurich]], Switzerland.

==Science education and the arts==
[[File:Zafra M Lerman students dancing to illustrate chemistry 2001 Gordon Conference (photo by David Morton).jpg|left|thumb|Zafra M Lerman students dancing to illustrate chemistry 2001 Gordon Conference (photo by David Morton)]]
Lerman used the arts to help teach science at all levels.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lerman|first1=Zafra|title=Using the Arts To Make Chemistry Accessible to Everybody. 2002 James Flack Norris Award, sponsored by ACS Northeast Section|journal=Journal of Chemical Education|department=Chemical & Engineering News|issue=v.80 i.11|publisher=American Chemical Society|date=November 1, 2003|volume=80|page=1234|doi=10.1021/ed080p1234|bibcode=2003JChEd..80.1234L |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lerman|first1=Zafra|title=Chemistry for art and communication students|journal=Journal of Chemical Education|date=February 1986|volume=63|issue=2|pages=142–143|doi=10.1021/ed063p142|bibcode=1986JChEd..63..142L}}</ref> In 1977, she became the first science faculty member at [[Columbia College Chicago]], an institution of higher education specializing in arts and media disciplines.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Daley|first1=Maraget|title=Silverstein resigns as life 'arts chair alter 3 1/2 years|url=http://digitalcommons.colum.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1014&context=cadc_chronicle|access-date=16 January 2016|agency=Columbia Chronicle|issue=6|publisher=Columbia College, Chicago|date=March 9, 1979}}</ref> In 1981, she founded the department of science and mathematics there and served as department chair through 1991.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Abdelaziz|first1=Fatma|title=Columbia adds Science department|url=http://digitalcommons.colum.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1034&context=cadc_chronicle|access-date=16 January 2016|agency=The Columbia Chronicle|publisher=Columbia College|date=March 20, 1981}}</ref> In 1991, she founded the Institute for Science Education and Science Communication (also known as the 'Science Institute") at Columbia College and served as its head until 2009.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Rodriguez|first1=Elizabeth|title=College president faces final term - A Chronicle exclusivi: An interview with Mike Alexandroff|url=http://digitalcommons.colum.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1135&context=cadc_chronicle|access-date=16 January 2016|agency=The Columbia Chronicle|publisher=Columbia College, Chicago|date=February 17, 1992}}</ref> Since 1991 she was a Distinguished Professor of Science and Public Policy.

Part of her teaching philosophy is captured in this quote, from a 2011 lecture entitled "Creativity in 3D: "Drawing, Dance, and Drama":
''"Students remember and understand abstract concepts best by producing their own artistic projects and using their own (sometimes hidden) creativity. Through this process, students are active learners, and utilize both their left and right brain, instead of being just passive observers."''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.icieworld.net/main1/images/stories/conf/ICIE_Istanbul_Program_online.pdf|title=2011 ICIE Conference|website=icieworld.net}}</ref>

==Peace activism==
[[File:HRH PrinceHassan (Jordan), Irina Bokova (UNESCO), Zafra M. Lerman at the Malta Conference V (Paris).jpg|thumb|Malta V Conference at UNESCO headquarters in Paris, France, December 4, 2011; His Royal Highness [[Prince Hassan bin Talal|Prince Hassan]] of Jordan (center-left), [[Irina Bokova]] (center-right, Director-general of UNESCO), and Dr. Zafra M. Lerman (right, President of the Malta Conferences Foundation). (Photo by Cynthia Warren Mentz)]]  In addition to developing innovative methods of teaching science through the arts, Lerman started using science to promote peace and human rights around the globe. In 1986 she was named chair of the American Chemical Society's Subcommittee on Scientific Freedom and Human Rights.<ref>{{cite news|title=Columbia People|url=http://digitalcommons.colum.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1025&context=alumnae_news|access-date=16 January 2016|agency=Columbia College Alumni News|publisher=Columbia College, Chicago|date=Spring 1995}}</ref> Among other activities, this group's mission included helping scientists who, for political reasons, were jailed, abused, and sentenced to execution. She held that position for 25 years.

Starting in 2001, Lerman began working to develop a scientific conference that would bring together researchers from many different, often mutually hostile, nations in the [[Middle East]] so they could cooperatively work toward solving problems facing the region. With support from the [[American Chemical Society]] (ACS), [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry]] (IUPAC), the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (RSC - England), and the [[Gesellschaft Deutscher Chemiker]], the first conference was held on the island of [[Malta]] from December 6 to 11, 2003.<ref name="MaltaI">{{cite news|last1=Freemantle|first1=Michael|title=Middle Easterners Meet in Malta - Chemistry symposium aims to forge scientific links in a troubled region|url=http://pubs.acs.org/isubscribe/journals/cen/81/i50/html/8150notw8.html|access-date=16 January 2016|agency=Chemical & Engineering News|issue=v.81 i.50|publisher=American Chemical Society|date=December 15, 2003}}</ref><ref name="CEN-204-0112">{{cite news|last1=Freemantle|first1=Michael|title=Rendezvous in the Mediterranean: Chemistry symposium in Malta promotes cooperation in troubled Middle East|url=http://pubs.acs.org/isubscribe/journals/cen/82/i02/html/8202sci1.html|access-date=16 January 2016|agency=Chemistry and Engineering News|issue=v80 i02|publisher=American Chemical Society|date=January 12, 2004}}</ref> Attendees included six Nobel Laureates and scientists from 15 Middle Eastern Countries ([[Bahrain]], [[Egypt]], [[Iran]], [[Iraq]], [[Israel]], [[Jordan]], [[Kuwait]], [[Lebanon]], [[Libya]], [[Palestinian Authority]], [[Qatar]], [[Saudi Arabia]], [[Syria]], [[Turkey]], and [[United Arab Emirates]]).<ref name=CEN-204-0112 /> The conference included workshops to foster cross-border collaborations on air and water quality, science education for all, and green energy.

The organizers followed up by hosting a second meeting two years later, Malta II.<ref name="MaltaII">{{cite news|last1=Ritter|first1=Stephen K.|title=Science For Peace In The Middle East: Malta conference aims to strengthen scientific ties in troubled region|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/83/i46/Science-Peace-Middle-East.html|access-date=16 January 2016|agency=Chemical & Engineering News|issue=v.83 i.46|publisher=American Chemical Society|date=November 10, 2005|page=15}}</ref>

The meeting was honored by [[United States]] [[Senator]] [[Dick Durbin]] in a speech on the floor of the U.S. Senate entitled "Chemists Working Cooperatively".<ref name="Durbin2004">{{cite journal|last1=Durbin|first1=Richard|title=Chemists Working Cooperatively|journal=United States Congressional Record|date=May 12, 2004|volume=150|issue=66|pages=S5368–S5369|url=https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/CREC-2004-05-12/html/CREC-2004-05-12-pt1-PgS5368-2.htm}}</ref>

Lerman led the initiative to continue with the conferences and founded the Malta Conferences Foundation to support them. She secured the support of [[UNESCO]], the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization.
